The technical description of the game itself shows that it is an experience marked by partial observability, limited camera view, fog of war, high decision density and strong context dependence, so that the player perceives only a contingent fraction of the actual state of the match <1>Jalovaara</1><2>(Jalovaara, 2024, p. 12)</2>.

The problem is not merely empirical but methodological, because the analytical modeling of the game state itself requires simplifications and representation choices capable of making a high-dimensional and multimodal state space tractable, without thereby eliminating the underlying complexity of the competitive environment <1>Jalovaara</1><2>(Jalovaara, 2024, p. 23)</2>.

The picture becomes more serious once one notes that, even in matches governed by a matchmaking system designed to give both teams roughly equal chances, pre-game prediction studies achieve significant levels of accuracy from variables such as the draft, performance history and the player's proficiency with the chosen champion, which shows that the match does not begin on a competitive tabula rasa, but on a prior distribution of probabilities <1>Jalovaara</1><2>(Jalovaara, 2024, p. 17-18)</2>.

Moreover, simple aggregate statistics, such as the raw win rate, are not a reliable basis for comparing strategic decisions, precisely because the environment is permeated by selection bias: certain actions are chosen when the player is already ahead and others as a last resort in desperate situations, which artificially inflates or depresses their apparent results <1>Jalovaara</1><2>(Jalovaara, 2024, p. 7; p. 24)</2>.

Perttu Jalovaara is a researcher at Aalto University School of Science, where he wrote, in the context of the Master’s Programme in Mathematics and Operations Research, a dissertation on win probability estimation in esports, with a specific focus on League of Legends <1>Jalovaara</1><2>(Jalovaara, 2024, p. 3)</2>.

His work belongs to the field of esports analytics and is useful here because it offers a quantitative and methodologically rigorous treatment of problems of reading performance, context and strategic decision-making in a competitive digital environment, especially in showing that simple aggregate statistics are insufficient and that the game's variables require analytical contextualization <1>Jalovaara</1><2>(Jalovaara, 2024, p. 7)</2>.

This is what happens, for example, in banking packages with countless products that do not correspond to one another, making it “very difficult for the consumer to compare the benefit packages offered by banks” <1>Wada</1><2>(Wada, 2016, p. 168-169)</2>.

An abusive practice may occur when there is material interference with the consumer's capacity to understand the terms and conditions of the product or service, with an excessive advantage obtained from the lack of understanding of the risks, costs or conditions involved <1>Wada</1><2>(Wada, 2016, p. 141-142)</2>.

This requirement takes on particular weight in the prior estimate, a qualified moment of decision in which the consumer can examine “the quality of the service, the execution deadline, the materials used”, in short, the essential elements that make up the price and the substance of the performance, and can also clear up doubts and negotiate the terms before becoming bound <1>Wada</1><2>(Wada, 2016, p. 211)</2>.

When the structure of the offer “reduces price transparency”, “the comparability of offers” is hindered <1>Wada</1><2>(Wada, 2016, p. 168)</2>, which directly undermines freedom of choice in practice.

Prior information and express authorization perform a rebalancing function: they do not merely communicate, they make the execution of the performance conditional on a minimum form of verifiability by the recipient, offsetting the structural imbalance of the consumer relationship <1>Wada</1><2>(Wada, 2016, p. 210)</2>.

Wada makes this explicit by stating that there is abuse when there is an “alteration of the obligations set out in the estimate without the consumer's agreement” <1>Wada</1><2>(Wada, 2016, p. 55)</2>.

The same reasoning is reinforced when the author associates abusiveness with the element of surprise and with the lack of understanding of financial impacts, showing that an apparently transparent relationship may still be unlawful if it holds unexpected conditions in reserve for the consumer, since surprise prevents effective control over the scope of the commitment undertaken <1>Wada</1><2>(Wada, 2016, p. 120; p. 142)</2>.
